chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) judged regarding a concubine of a man who gave birth to a son for her master. Then he separated from her, so he married her to his slave. Then her master died and emancipated her. So her son inherited her husband from his father. Then her son died, so she inherited her husband from her son. So they came disputing, the man saying, 'She is my wife, and I have not divorced her,' and the woman saying, 'He is my slave, and he should not copulate with me.'

So the woman said, 'O Amir al-Mu'minin! My master kept me as a concubine, so he made me give birth to a son. Then he separated from me, and married me to this slave of his. So when death presented itself to my master, he emancipated me at his death, and I am the wife of this one, and he has become a slave owned by my son whom I bore from my master. And my son died, so I inherited him. Is it correct for him to copulate with me?'

He said to her, 'Has he copulated with you since he became your slave and you were willing?' She said, 'No, O Amir al-Mu'minin.' He said, 'If you had done it, I would have stoned you. Go, for he is your slave. There is no authority for him upon you. If you wish, you can sell him; if you wish, you can manumit him; if you wish, you can emancipate him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a wife who inherits her slave-husband from her son?
ai.summary: This ruling from Imam Ali (AS) in *Al-Kafi* elucidates the legal distinction between *umm al-walad* status and marital ownership, specifically addressing the rights of a free woman who inherits her slave-husband. The Imam’s condition of voluntary cohabitation (*jamāʿ*) highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that emancipation or inheritance does not automatically grant the slave conjugal rights without the owner's consent, preserving her autonomy. This case is frequently cited in *fiqh* discussions regarding the interplay of *kitābah* (manumission contract) and *nikāḥ* (marriage) in classical Shia legal theory.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Najra, from Aasim Bin Humeyr, from Muhammad Bin Qays, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup> judged regarding a concubine of a man who gave birth for her master. Then he isolated from her, so his slave married her. Then her master died and emancipated her. So her inherited her husband from his father. Then her son died, so she inherited her husband from her son. So they went on to dispute. The man was saying, ‘She is my wife, and I have not divorced her’, and the wife was saying, ‘He is my slave he should not be copulating with me’.

So the woman said, ‘O Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup>! My master had kept me as a concubine, so he made me give birth to a son. Then he isolated from me, and got me married to this slave of his. So when the death presented itself to my master, he emancipated me during his death, and I am a wife of this one, and he has become an owned slave of my son whom I gave birth to from my master. And then my son dies, so I inherited him. Is it correct for him that he sleeps with me?’

So he<sup>asws</sup> said to her: ‘Has he slept with you since he came to be your slave and you were willing?’ She said, ‘No, O Amir Al-Momineen<sup>asws</sup>!’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Had you done it, you would have been stoned. Go, for he is your slave. There is no way for him upon you. If you so desire to you sell him, and if you so desire to you leave him, and if you so desire to you emancipate him’.
